title: Emphasis and information flow: cumulative review
objectives: Use anticipatory it with a that-clause or infinitive.
Distinguish anticipatory it from a cleft.
Apply earlier structures to information flow.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A text is easier to follow when its sentences connect information the reader already has with information the writer wants to add. Writers can place an established topic near the beginning and a significant new detail near the end. This tendency is useful, not a compulsory rule. The best order depends on what the audience knows and what the writer wants to emphasise.

Compare “A new library will open beside the station” with “Beside the station, a new library will open.” The second version establishes the location first. If the station area is already the topic of a discussion, that order can make the connection especially clear.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: One way to delay a long subject is to begin with anticipatory it: “It is surprising that the plans changed.” Here it does not refer to an object. The later that-clause supplies the content that is surprising. The alternative “That the plans changed is surprising” is grammatical but can feel heavier at the start.

A similar construction uses a preparatory it with an adjective and an infinitive: “It is difficult to compare the results.” This wording does not identify a specific person doing the comparing unless the context does so or a phrase such as for the researchers is added. Do not confuse anticipatory it with it referring back to a particular noun.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: A writer can also use structures studied earlier to manage focus. “It was the second report that changed the decision” highlights the second report. “The first report we can use; the second needs revision” fronts an object to establish a contrast. “Only after the meeting did we understand” places a restriction first and uses inversion in the main clause.

A formal conditional can be fronted too: “Had the team checked, it might have found the error.” The condition sets the frame for the result. These structures have different grammatical forms and different discourse effects; they are not interchangeable merely because they all move information towards the beginning.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not treat anticipatory it as an it-cleft in every sentence beginning with it is or it was. In “It was surprising that the plan changed”, the that-clause supplies the content evaluated as surprising. In “It was the plan that changed”, the phrase the plan is the focused element of a cleft. The two constructions perform different jobs.

A long introductory phrase can help a reader, but too many fronted or inverted clauses can make prose hard to process. Prefer ordinary order when it fits the context. Also remember that the auxiliary moves before the subject after initial only after, whereas a fronted object such as the first report normally leaves subject–verb order unchanged.

examples.sentence: It is surprising that the plans changed.
examples.note: Anticipatory it introduces a later content clause.

examples.sentence: That the plans changed is surprising.
examples.note: The content clause is the grammatical subject in this heavier opening.

examples.sentence: It is difficult to compare the results.
Beside the station, a new library will open.
examples.note: The location frames the new information.

examples.sentence: It was the second report that changed the decision.
examples.note: The cleft focuses the second report.

examples.sentence: The first report we can use; the second needs revision.
examples.note: A fronted object establishes a comparison.

examples.sentence: Only after the meeting did we understand.
examples.note: The restrictive phrase triggers main-clause inversion.

examples.sentence: Had the team checked, it might have found the error.
examples.note: The inverted condition sets a hypothetical frame.

common_errors.incorrect: It is difficult compare the results.
common_errors.correct: It is difficult to compare the results.
common_errors.reason: The adjective pattern uses an infinitive with to.

common_errors.incorrect: Only after the meeting we did understand.
common_errors.correct: Only after the meeting did we understand.
common_errors.reason: Put the auxiliary before the subject after the fronted restrictive phrase.

common_errors.incorrect: The first report we can use it.
common_errors.correct: The first report we can use.
common_errors.reason: Do not repeat the fronted object with it in this standard written construction.

summary: Anticipatory it can introduce a content or infinitive clause later in the sentence.
Use fronting and clefts to shape topic, contrast and focus.
Match inversion to its trigger and choose structures that help the audience.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence with anticipatory it.
exercises.explanation: It anticipates the content clause that the plans changed.

options.text: It was the guide who spoke.
It is surprising that the plans changed.
It was the plan that changed.
It was Mina who called.

option_feedback.a: “It was the guide who spoke.” does not fit here. It anticipates the content clause that the plans changed.
option_feedback.b: “It is surprising that the plans changed.” fits here. It anticipates the content clause that the plans changed.
option_feedback.c: “It was the plan that changed.” does not fit here. It anticipates the content clause that the plans changed.
option_feedback.d: “It was Mina who called.” does not fit here. It anticipates the content clause that the plans changed.

exercises.explanation: Difficult is followed by the to-infinitive here.

option_feedback.d: “to compare” fits here. Difficult is followed by the to-infinitive here.

option_feedback.c: “It is difficult to read the report.” does not fit here. The second report occupies the focus position in the cleft.
option_feedback.d: “It seems that the report changed.” does not fit here. The second report occupies the focus position in the cleft.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly fronts a restrictive phrase?
exercises.explanation: Did precedes the subject in the main clause after only after.

options.text: Only after the meeting we understood did.
Only after did the meeting we understand.
Only after the meeting did we understand.
Only after the meeting we did understood.

option_feedback.a: “Only after the meeting we understood did.” does not fit here. Did precedes the subject in the main clause after only after.
option_feedback.b: “Only after did the meeting we understand.” does not fit here. Did precedes the subject in the main clause after only after.
option_feedback.c: “Only after the meeting did we understand.” fits here. Did precedes the subject in the main clause after only after.
option_feedback.d: “Only after the meeting we did understood.” does not fit here. Did precedes the subject in the main clause after only after.

exercises.prompt: Choose a formal inverted past condition.
exercises.explanation: Had precedes the subject and checked is the past participle.

options.text: If had the team checked, it would have found it.
Had the team check, it might found it.
Should the team checked, it might found it.
Had the team checked, it might have found it.

option_feedback.a: “If had the team checked, it would have found it.” does not fit here. Had precedes the subject and checked is the past participle.
option_feedback.b: “Had the team check, it might found it.” does not fit here. Had precedes the subject and checked is the past participle.
option_feedback.c: “Should the team checked, it might found it.” does not fit here. Had precedes the subject and checked is the past participle.
option_feedback.d: “Had the team checked, it might have found it.” fits here. Had precedes the subject and checked is the past participle.

exercises.prompt: What the guests need ___ a quiet room. Use is.
exercises.explanation: Is links the what-clause to its complement.

exercises.prompt: Rarely ___ they arrive late. Use did.
exercises.explanation: Initial rarely triggers inversion with did.
